title: How acoustic recording worked at Gennett
summary: Chubb-Steinberg's contract with Gennett; he explains wax discs, recording horns, and burning the wax to make a second take.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Well he didn't stay around there very long and you stayed--- he left after a few months but you stayed on there with Chubby Steinberg and you started --- Tell about the recordings at Richmond, Indiana, the Gennetts ---

Well, we recorded--- our band started to--- we got a contract with Gennett -- and, of course, you know - to do a side were you to play one song at that time, was a real test--- sometimes it would take you a whole bloody session to do one number because, of course, you know there was no electric and you played through tin-horns into long pieces of hose going into this hugh thing with a needle on it and the discs were about - about what would you that would be -- about?
---and they were on a big turn-table and, uh, if you made a mistake, you could only make one on that wax. The wax was about an inch-and-a-half to two

inches thick - the piece of wax. Now, if you made a mistake, they had a gas thing - the same size as that in a funnel shape thing with gas jets burning -- and if you made a mistake, they'd--- that was okay for that one -- they would bring this big cone shaped thing down by the burning gas and they would burn a new soft surface on that---
It would burn the other stuff off---
It would just melt a clean surface on it.
In effect, you had to start all over again.
Oh, yes. But, you could only do that once. If we made two mistakes that piece of wax could--- well, it couldn't be used until it was machined-
See, they had to machine it down; because once you've melt -- the end wax will turn down a little and that would be what would spoil it. But, uh, ---
